title: Narrative Characteristics of Captivating Secondary Mathematics Lessons https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10649-022-10184-y atics-lessons/
author: Barton, Craig
source: Tips for Teachers (tipsforteachers.co.uk), February 25, 2025 — original paper:
summary: Barton covers Dietiker et al.'s study analyzing why some secondary maths lessons captivate students while others fall flat, using a 'mathematical story' framework applied to lesson observations and student surveys across multiple schools. The researchers identified eight narrative characteristics that separate captivating lessons from dull ones, including how many questions stay open across the lesson and how often 'misdirection' occurs — moments where a student's false assumption leads to a surprising result. Captivating lessons tended to keep mathematical questions open across multiple 'acts' of the lesson rather than resolving them quickly, and used more misdirection to build tension before a satisfying reveal. Barton draws out that this is about deliberate lesson sequencing and pacing, not content difficulty — the same mathematical content can be told as a dull sequence of steps or as a story with real tension and payoff.
points: Captivating lessons keep mathematical questions open across multiple parts of the lesson rather than resolving them immediately — the tension between known and unknown is what sustains interest.

Misdirection — deliberately letting students' false assumptions lead to a surprising result — appeared more often in lessons students rated as captivating, though the study cautions it must be used carefully.
The narrative-design lens applies to sequencing existing content, not to inventing new material — the same maths topic can be told as a flat procedure or as a story with real tension and a payoff.
Effectiveness of these techniques still depends on context: teachers need to weigh their own students' prior experiences and classroom personality before applying a given narrative structure.
quotes: Secondary mathematics classrooms can be sites of delightful claims ('Yo! N and I go together!'), surprise ('Woah!'), and excitement ('That's crazy!') for students
The study showed that lessons with broad appeal had mathematical questions that remained open for multiple acts, spanned more of the story, and offered incremental progress throughout the lesson.

While the study found misdirection was more common in captivating lessons, teachers should use it carefully. Misdirection, like equivocations, snares, and jammings, can increase tension and lead to surprise when the truth is revealed.
Lessons should provide opportunities for wonderment and surprise to prevent students from seeing mathematics as boring.
A student's experience depends on how the story is told, specifically how the tension between the known and unknown shifts across the lesson.
